fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over a category \mathcal {C} and another displayed category \overline {\mathcal {D}} over \int \overline {\mathcal {C}}, the total category of \overline {\mathcal {C}}, we can define \overline {\int } \overline {\mathcal {D}}, the displayed total category of \overline {\mathcal {D}}, as a displayed category over \mathcal {C}.

fr:title.text: Pi types in displayed categories require Conduché fibrations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Pi types in displayed categories require Conduché fibrations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Displayed categories model parts of a dependent type theory. Categories are contexts; displayed categories are dependent types.

html:ul.html:li: C^{\mathtt {D}} : \mathsf {Category}^{\mathtt {D}}\, C corresponds to C \vdash C^{\mathtt {D}}\ \mathsf {Type}.
\int C^{\mathtt {D}} : \mathsf {Category} corresponds to C, x : C^{\mathtt {D}}\ \mathsf {Ctx} — this is the total category.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Many of the operations of dependent type theory transfer cleanly to the displayed-category side. But Max claims that in general we cannot form a Pi type unless the associated displayed category is a Conduché fibration. Is this true, and if so, why?

A \Pi -type along a display map C^{\mathtt {D}} \to C is, categorically, a right adjoint to the substitution/pullback functor that reindexes displayed objects along that projection. So existence of \Pi -types is existence of a right adjoint to {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} \times _{C} \int C^{\mathtt {D}} on the slice — equivalently, exponentiability of the projection \int C^{\mathtt {D}} \to C viewed as an arrow in \mathbf {Cat}.

Conduché's theorem. A functor p : E \to B is exponentiable in \mathbf {Cat} iff it is a Conduché fibration: for every morphism u : e \to e' in E and every factorization p{\mathopen {}\left (u\right )\mathclose {}} = g \circ f in B, there exists an essentially unique factorization u = v \circ w in E with p{\mathopen {}\left (w\right )\mathclose {}} = f and p{\mathopen {}\left (v\right )\mathclose {}} = g.

fr:title.text: Why the weaker classes don't suffice

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the weaker classes don't suffice

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cloven (Grothendieck) fibrations give \Pi -types when they are closed under dependent products in a stronger sense (i.e. they are \Pi -fibrations in the Jacobs sense, [jacobs-1999] Ch.~9). Generic displayed categories are weaker than fibrations, and even fibrations do not automatically give exponentiability of the total projection. Conduché is precisely the condition that fixes this for the underlying functor in \mathbf {Cat}.

Concretely, the Conduché condition lets us lift factorizations of substitutions in the base to factorizations of morphisms upstairs. Building a generic element of \Pi x{:}A.\, B requires assembling, for each substitution \sigma : \Gamma ' \to \Gamma , a coherent family of sections over A{\mathopen {}\llbracket \sigma \rrbracket \mathclose {}}; checking that two such families agree under further substitution requires matching up factorizations on the nose. This is exactly what fails without Conduché.

html:ul.html:li: Track down the precise statement and reference. Streicher's Fibered Categories à la Bénabou and Jacobs's Categorical Logic and Type Theory are the obvious sources.
Conduché's original paper (1972) for exponentiability = Conduché-fibration.

Reconcile with the standard display map / comprehension category presentations: in those settings \Pi -types are usually stipulated by asking the relevant pullback functor to have a right adjoint, which implicitly imposes exponentiability when one tries to construct examples in \mathbf {Cat}.
Confirm with Max that "in general we cannot have a Pi type" means "existence of \Pi -types in the resulting displayed type theory forces Conduché on the projection", not the reverse implication.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a functor F : \mathcal {C} \to \mathcal {D}, we can define a displayed category of fibers along F up to isomorphism using the reindexing construction on the displayed category of isomorphisms.

First we can reindex the category of isomorphisms to get \mathsf {reindex}_{\mathsf {Id} \times F}{\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {Iso_{D}}\right )\mathclose {}}, a displayed category over \mathcal {D} \times \mathcal {C}. Then using the observation that product categories arise as total categories, we can invoke the displayed total category construction to repackage the data of \mathsf {reindex}_{\mathsf {Id} \times F}{\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {Iso_{D}}\right )\mathclose {}} as a category displayed over \mathcal {D}, which we call \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}}.

\mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}} has the universal property that a global section of it comprises the same data as a section of F. That is, a section of \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}} gives the ingredients to construct a functor G : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C} such that F \circ G \cong \mathsf {Id}.

A category \mathcal {C} consists of
A type of objects \mathcal {C}_{0}
For each pair of objects x , y : \mathcal {C}_{0} a set of morphisms \mathcal {C} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}}. We may simply write a moprhism with an arrow, denote f : \mathcal {C} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}} as f : x \to y or x \overset {f}{\to } y or similar
A composition operation on morphisms. For f : x \to y and g : y \to z, there is a morphism f \star g : x \to z
For each x : \mathcal {c}_{0}, an identity morphism \mathsf {id}_{x} : x \to x
Left-unitality of composition: for all f : x \to y, an equality \mathsf {idL}_{f} : \mathsf {id}_{x} \star f = f
Right-unitality of composition: for all f : x \to y, an equality \mathsf {idR}_{f} : f \star \mathsf {id}_{y} = f
Associativity of composition: for all f : x \to y, g : y \to z, h : z \to w, an equality \mathsf {assoc}_{f , g , h} : {\mathopen {}\left (f \star {\mathopen {}\left (g \star h\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}} = {\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (f \star g\right )\mathclose {}} \star h\right )\mathclose {}}
Concretely, the definition above is meant to model the one used in the Cubical standard libary [cubicalagdalib].

However, the notion of category is flexible. Depending on the context, we may be talking of small , locally small, wild, or any other kind of category that may augment which things we require to be (homotopy) sets, which things we require to be small types, etc. For the most part, the same idea of a category will apply across all of these settings.

Because the type \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{f}{\mathopen {}\left (\overline {x} , \overline {y}\right )\mathclose {}} of displayed morphisms depends on the base morphism f, the two sides of each displayed law inhabit different displayed hom-sets — those indexed by the two sides of the corresponding base-category equation. Each displayed law is therefore a heterogeneous equality a =_{p} b: a path from a to b lying over the base path p, rather than an equation within a single fixed set.
Concretely, this definition models the one used in the Cubical standard library [cubicalagdalib].

A displayed category is to a category as a dependent type is to a context. In this way, displayed categories are effectively dependent categories, as we present the structure of \overline {\mathcal {D}} as a category parametrized by the structure of \mathcal {C}.

Displayed categories were introduced by Ahrens and Lumsdaine [ahrens-lumsdaine-2019]. The point is that a displayed category over \mathcal {C} is equivalent to the data of a category \mathcal {D} together with a functor F : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C}, but presented as families indexed by the objects and morphisms of \mathcal {C} — so that constructions like Grothendieck fibrations can be defined without ever invoking equality of objects.
